# Pronouncing Asanga: a guide for the curious

Saying **Asanga** aloud requires more than reading Latin letters ​on a screen. The conventional spelling is only the entry point into a reconstructed sound and a much older tradition. This post unpacks that sound, the Devanagari evidence, the kindred forms, and the ‌mythological record, then shows how the temple preserves the whole argument without pretending that a diacritic was ever lost.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Asanga
- **ASCII form:** asanga
- **Meaning:** "Without attachment"
- **Domain of ‌influence:** Yogacara, Mind-Only
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** असन्ग (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Asanga** (*asanga*) — Yogacara, Mind-Only · Without attachment — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under ​the domain "Yogacara, Mind-Only". The name means "Without attachment".

**Asanga** (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the founder of **Yogācāra**, the Buddhist school that analyzed consciousness itself — the *ālayavijñāna* store-mind, the three natures, ​the construction of the world by perception — and the man who, by tradition, received the future Buddha Maitreya's five treatises on a visit to Tuṣita heaven.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling ​**Asanga** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/asanga/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *asanga* contains the same letters: no recovered ​diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## Mythology

The stories of Asanga place yogacara, mind-only at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Asanga appears in buddhist tradition as yogacara, mind-only. ​The name's meaning, "Without attachment", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Asanga in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the ​modern scholarly record.

The myths of Asanga survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not ​privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Asanga gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Two Brothers, One Teaching (The ​Brothers)

Asanga and his younger half-brother **Vasubandhu** — arguably the two most consequential Buddhist philosophers after Nāgārjuna — were born, the story runs (Xuanzang preserves it in his *Great Tang Records of the ​Western Regions*), to a brahmin of Kauśika lineage; their mother, the legend adds, resolved that one son should master the Mahāyāna and the other its rival, the analytical Abhidharma of Kaśmīr. Vasubandhu became ‌the encyclopedist of the *Abhidharmakośa*; Asanga wandered and meditated until he founded **Yogācāra**. Then the elder brother executed the gentlest ambush in the history of ideas: feigning a mortal illness, he had ​disciples read him a Mahāyāna sūtra and plant objections that only the Mahāyāna could answer — until the great critic recanted on the spot and joined the school he had spent his career ‌refuting. Vasubandhu's conversion doubled the school's firepower: the *Viṃśikā* and *Trimśikā* became its core. The myth explains a real fact: **half of the Indian Mahāyāna was written by one family** — brotherly love ​as the engine of a philosophical revolution.

### Twelve Years, a Wounded Dog, and Maitreya (The Vision)

The founding vision of Yogācāra is a story about **compassion first**. Asanga, the tradition says (Xuanzang; the ‌Tibetan historians Bu ston and Tāranātha repeat it), spent **twelve years** in solitary retreat awaiting a vision of the future Buddha **Maitreya** — and saw nothing. Despairing on his way down the mountain, ​he met a dog dying in the road, its open wounds alive with maggots; to save both creature and worms he cut flesh from his own thigh and reached to lift the maggots ‌with his tongue. The dog vanished: it was **Maitreya**. The bodhisattva then carried Asanga bodily to **Tuṣita heaven**, where he received the five great treatises — *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, *Madhyāntavibhāga*, *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*, *Ratnagotravibhāga*. Modern ​scholarship — Frauwallner most forcefully — argues Asanga wrote them himself. The interpretive point survives either way: a philosophy of mind founded by a man whose breakthrough came through the **gut** — the ‌dying dog was the last rung of the ladder.

### Yogācāra, the Practice of Mind-Only (The School)

What Asanga built — with Vasubandhu and their lineage — the tradition called **Yogācāra**, "practice of yoga," ​and its opponents called *cittamātra*, "mind-only." Its masterworks, the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha* ("Compendium of the Mahāyāna") and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, set out a psychology of awakening: the **store-consciousness** (*ālayavijñāna*), a deep repository in which the seeds ​of deeds and habits sleep, waiting to sprout as the world; the **three natures** — the imagined (the snake), the dependent (the rope), the perfected (the seeing); and the radical claim that the ‌"external world" is a construction of consciousness, no more independent than a dream is independent of the dreamer. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* supplied the school's scriptural charter, with its doctrine of the three turnings ‌of the wheel. The interpretive meaning: suffering was re-described from metaphysics into **psychology** — and liberation as a rewiring of perception, perception seen at last as the whole stage.

## Symbols & Iconography

The ‌iconography associated with Asanga concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Asanga, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — ​Yogacara, Mind-Only

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Asanga across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about ​power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Asanga carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The wounded dog** — The dying dog whose maggots he moved with his tongue — the act of ‌compassion that revealed Maitreya, and the founding parable of Yogācāra: insight comes through the heart, not the head
- **Maitreya's tower** — Tuṣita heaven, where the five treatises were received — Yogācāra's scriptural charter ​is literally from the future
- **The mirror** — The school's favorite image in later East Asian art — perception like a mirror: images arise, none stick; Asanga's name, 'without attachment,' is the mirror ​wiped clean
- **The storehouse (ālaya)** — The ālayavijñāna, the warehouse consciousness where seeds of karma sleep and sprout — his school's most influential and most argued concept
- **The three natures** — Imagined, dependent, ‌perfected — Asanga's map of how the mind builds its world and how it sees through the building

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is ​yet assigned to Asanga with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Buddhist name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the ​textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming असन्ग, sanctuary or cult remains tied to yogacara and iconography ‌matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Asanga** is yogacara, mind-only. The name ​means "Without attachment" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Asanga returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Yogacara

Central domain: yogacara, mind-only.

### Living Tradition

Honored in buddhist myth, cult, and ‌cultural memory.

### Canonical Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple with its canonical scholarly spelling and supporting evidence.

### Yogācāra

The 'practice of yoga' school — Abhidharma rewritten as psychology: suffering located in the structure ​of consciousness itself.

### The Vision of Maitreya

Twelve years of retreat, a dying dog, and transport to Tuṣita heaven — where the future Buddha dictated the five great treatises.

### The Two Brothers

​He and his half-brother Vasubandhu wrote half the Indian Mahāyāna — the gentle ambush that converted the greatest critic of the Mahāyāna.

## A Meditation

Asanga's school asks the question most traditions bury: not 'what is the world?' ​but '**who is building it right now?**' His answer — the mind, constructing its world and mistaking the construction for the thing — was psychology three centuries before Augustine and fifteen before the ​laboratory. But his founding parable keeps the science honest: the vision came not from analysis but from a dying dog, and the first act of the school's founder was to bleed for a ‌stranger's wounds.

There is a lesson in the pairing. Yogācāra's map of mind — seeds, stores, three natures — is as intricate as any in antiquity, yet the tradition insists it was dictated ‌by compassion itself, in the form of Maitreya. Analysis without tenderness, Asanga's life says, is just another attachment — to being right. The name is the teaching: **without attachment**, even to the map. ‌A psychologist who knew that the last obstacle is the theory of the obstacle.
